Bread dough rises because yeast consumes sugars and releases carbon dioxide gas. As that gas collects inside the dough, it makes the dough expand. Gluten provides the structure that helps hold the gas in: a developed gluten network traps it so the dough can grow instead of simply letting it escape.

Temperature affects how quickly this happens. Within normal proofing temperatures, warmth generally speeds up yeast activity, so a warm dough rises faster. In cooler conditions, yeast works more slowly and the rise takes longer. That extra time can allow more flavor to develop. Excessive heat, however, can damage or kill the yeast.

Leaving dough to proof for too long can also cause trouble. Its structure may weaken until it can no longer hold the gas well, allowing the dough to lose volume or collapse. Because recipes and conditions vary, watch the dough’s expansion and texture rather than relying only on a fixed proofing time.
